questions.q: What is a bond?
options: A share of ownership in a company
A savings account at a bank
A loan you give to a government or company
questions.why: A loan to a government or company that is paid back with agreed payments.

questions.q: Who issues bonds?
questions.why: Governments and companies that want to borrow money.

questions.q: What happens if the issuer cannot pay?
options: You can lose part or all of what you lent
The state always pays you back instead
The bond turns into a share
questions.why: Investors can lose part or all of what they lent (default risk).

questions.q: Why can a bond's price fall before it matures?
options: Bonds lose value every day by law
questions.why: If newer bonds offer better payments, older ones become less attractive and their price drops.

questions.q: Who issues Polish retail savings bonds?
questions.why: The State Treasury.

questions.q: Which usually swings less: bonds or shares?
questions.why: Bonds.

questions.q: Why hold bonds next to shares?
options: They always earn more than shares
They usually swing less and soften falls
questions.why: They usually swing less, which can soften falls in a mixed portfolio.

questions.q: How much of your money would you want in calmer assets?
What is an investment fund?
options: Money from many people invested together
questions.why: A pot of money from many people, invested together by a manager.

questions.q: What is an index fund?
options: A fund whose manager picks hot stocks
A fund that copies an index
A fund that only holds cash
questions.why: A fund that copies an index instead of picking individual stocks.

questions.q: Why does an index fund give instant diversification?
options: It buys only the best company
It holds all companies in its index
It is guaranteed by the state
questions.why: It holds all the companies in its index, so one purchase spreads money across many.

questions.q: What does the MSCI World index cover?
options: Large and mid-size firms in many developed countries
questions.why: Large and mid-size companies across many developed countries.

questions.q: What is a fund's yearly fee (TER)?
options: A one-time fee when you buy
A tax paid to the state
The yearly cost as a % of your money
questions.why: The yearly cost of a fund as a % of your money, taken automatically.

questions.q: With 7% a year before fees, what is the difference after 20 years on 10,000 zl between a 0.2% and a 2% fee?
questions.why: About 10,700 zl (about 37,300 zl vs 26,500 zl).

questions.q: What is the legal cap on the management fee of Polish open-ended funds?
questions.why: 2.0% a year.

questions.q: Why do low-cost index funds often beat expensive active funds over time?
options: Fees are certain and compound; skill is not
Active funds are illegal in Poland
questions.why: Fees are certain and compound every year, while extra skill is uncertain.

questions.q: What is the 'behaviour gap'?
options: The gap between bond and share prices
Investors earn less due to badly timed trades
The time between buying and selling
questions.why: Investors earn less than their funds because of badly timed buying and selling: 8.7% vs 9.9% a year (US, 10 years to 2025).

questions.q: What is an ETF?
options: A fund traded on an exchange like a share
questions.why: A fund traded on a stock exchange like a share, usually tracking an index at low cost.

questions.q: How do you buy an ETF?
options: Only by phone from the fund manager
questions.why: Through a brokerage account, on a stock exchange, like a share.

questions.q: What do iShares Core MSCI World and Vanguard FTSE All-World cost a year?
What does ETFBW20TR on GPW track, and what does it cost?
questions.why: The WIG20TR index; 0.47% a year.

questions.q: Accumulating vs distributing ETF: what is the difference?
options: Accumulating reinvests dividends; distributing pays them out
questions.why: Accumulating reinvests dividends; distributing pays them out.

questions.q: Why check an ETF's currency?
options: Only euro ETFs can be bought in Poland
Currency moves add to your result
questions.why: A fund priced in another currency adds currency swings to your result.

questions.q: What should a first investing plan contain?
options: Amount, fund, day of month, review date
questions.why: An amount, a fund, a day of the month, and when you will review it.

questions.q: How much could you invest each month without stress?
What are the main ways to invest in real estate?
questions.why: Buying property directly, or buying property funds or REITs.

questions.q: What is a REIT?
options: A company or fund owning rental property, traded like a share
questions.why: A company or fund that owns income-producing property and trades like a share.

questions.q: Why is property called illiquid?
options: It is slow and costly to sell
questions.why: It can take months to sell, and buying and selling have high costs.

questions.q: What ongoing costs come with a rental flat?
options: Maintenance, repairs, taxes, insurance, empty months
questions.why: Maintenance, repairs, taxes, insurance and empty months.

questions.q: Why is one flat a concentrated investment?
options: It is spread across many cities
All money depends on one building and place
questions.why: All the money depends on one building in one location.

questions.q: How can a small investor spread property risk?
options: Property funds or REITs with many buildings
questions.why: Through property funds or REITs that hold many buildings.

questions.q: What are money market securities?
options: Very short-term loans, usually a year or less
questions.why: Very short-term loans to governments, banks and companies, usually a year or less.

questions.q: What is a money market fund?
options: A fund of short-term securities aiming for stable value
questions.why: A fund that holds short-term securities to keep its value stable.

questions.q: What does 'real return' mean?
questions.why: The return after subtracting inflation.

questions.q: If inflation is 3.5% (GUS, Oct 2026) and your cash earns 3.0%, what is your real return?
questions.why: About -0.5%: you lose buying power.

questions.q: What is short-term cash best used for?
options: Emergency fund and money needed soon
questions.why: An emergency fund and money you need soon.

questions.q: What is a common guideline for the size of an emergency fund?
options: About 3 to 6 months of essential costs
questions.why: Around 3 to 6 months of essential expenses (a rule of thumb, not a law).

questions.q: What is a bank deposit?
options: Money placed with a bank for a set time at an agreed rate
A loan the bank gives you
questions.why: Money placed with a bank for a set time at an agreed rate.

questions.q: How are bank deposits protected in Poland?
options: They are not protected at all
BFG covers up to EUR 100,000 per person per bank
questions.why: The Bank Guarantee Fund (BFG) covers up to the PLN equivalent of EUR 100,000 per person per bank.

questions.q: What does 'guaranteed' usually mean in an insurance product?
options: You can never lose any money anywhere
A minimum value or payout under contract terms
questions.why: The insurer promises a minimum value or payout under the contract terms.

questions.q: What is the usual trade-off for a guarantee?
options: Lower growth, often higher fees or lock-up
questions.why: Lower expected growth, and often higher fees or a lock-up period.

questions.q: What is the main risk of 'safe' products?
options: Returns below inflation shrink buying power
questions.why: Their return can fall below inflation, so your buying power shrinks.

questions.q: What does 'guaranteed high return' usually signal?
questions.why: A red flag: real investments with high returns always carry risk.

questions.q: How do you check a seller is licensed?
options: KNF register and KNF warning list
questions.why: Search the KNF register of supervised entities and the KNF public warning list.

questions.q: What is an option?
options: The right, not obligation, to buy or sell at a set price
An obligation to buy at any price
questions.why: A contract giving the right, but not the obligation, to buy or sell something at a set price before a set date.

questions.q: Call vs put: what is the difference?
options: Call = right to buy; put = right to sell
questions.why: A call is the right to buy; a put is the right to sell.

questions.q: What can happen to the money paid for an option?
questions.why: The option can expire worthless, losing 100% of it.

questions.q: Why are options called leveraged?
options: Small price moves cause large % gains or losses
questions.why: Small price moves cause large percentage gains or losses.

questions.q: What is hedging?
options: Buying more of the same stock
Reducing the risk of a position you hold
questions.why: Using a contract to reduce the risk of a position you already hold.

questions.q: Are options suited to beginners building long-term savings?
options: Yes, they are the safest start
questions.why: Generally no: they are complex and can lose value fast.

questions.q: What is a futures contract?
options: An agreement to buy or sell at a set price on a future date
questions.why: An agreement to buy or sell something at a set price on a future date; both sides must follow through.

questions.q: Option vs future: what is the key difference?
options: Future is a right; option is an obligation
Option is a right; future is an obligation
questions.why: An option is a right; a future is an obligation.

questions.q: What is margin?
options: A fee paid once a year
A deposit you must keep; you may need to add money
questions.why: A deposit you must keep to hold the position; if prices move against you, you must add money.

questions.q: Can you lose more than you put in with leveraged futures?
questions.why: Yes, losses can exceed the initial deposit.

questions.q: Why do farmers or airlines use futures?
options: To lock in prices and reduce uncertainty
questions.why: To lock in prices and reduce uncertainty.

questions.q: What is a CFD?
options: A leveraged contract on an asset's price difference
questions.why: A contract that pays the price difference of an asset without owning it, usually with leverage.

questions.q: An ad promises 'easy profits trading CFDs'. What do you do?
options: Check the firm in the KNF register first
feedback: CFDs are leveraged; most retail traders lose money. 'Easy profits' is a red flag.
Good habit: check the licence and the KNF warning list before anything.
Fine choice: there's no need to trade leveraged products to build savings.

questions.q: What is an exchange rate?
options: The price of one currency in another
questions.why: The price of one currency in another, e.g. EUR/PLN.

questions.q: What was the NBP EUR/PLN mid rate on 19 Nov 2026?
questions.why: 4.4165 zl per euro.

questions.q: You buy a US fund in zloty and the dollar weakens. What happens?
questions.why: Your result in zloty falls, even if the fund's dollar price is unchanged.

questions.q: What is a PLN-hedged fund?
options: It reduces currency effects on your zloty result
questions.why: A fund that reduces the effect of currency moves on your zloty result.

questions.q: What is a currency conversion fee?
options: A cost for changing zloty into another currency
questions.why: A cost for changing zloty into another currency to buy foreign assets.

questions.q: Why is currency trading risky for beginners?
options: Often leveraged and news-driven, so losses come fast
It is only for banks by law
questions.why: It is often leveraged and prices jump on news, so losses can be fast.

questions.q: How is gold usually used in a portfolio?
options: As a store of value not tied to any company
questions.why: As a store of value that does not depend on any company; its price can still swing a lot.

questions.q: What was the NBP gold price on 20 Nov 2026?
questions.why: 481.23 zl per gram.

questions.q: What are common ways to own gold?
options: Bars or coins, or funds tracking gold
questions.why: Physical bars or coins, or funds that track the gold price.

questions.q: What extra costs come with physical gold?
questions.why: The dealer's gap between buy and sell prices, plus safe storage.

questions.q: Does gold pay dividends?
questions.why: No. Its return comes only from price changes.

questions.q: Does the gold price always rise?
options: No, it can fall for years
questions.why: No. It can fall and stay low for years.

questions.q: Would you hold some gold, and why?
options: A small part, as a store of value

questions.q: What is variable life insurance?
options: Life cover plus fund investments whose value moves
questions.why: Life cover combined with investments in funds; its value moves with those funds.

questions.q: What is an annuity?
options: A contract turning savings into regular payments
questions.why: A contract that turns savings into regular payments, often for life.

questions.q: Why compare fees carefully on these products?
options: Fees are set by law to zero
Wrappers can add fee layers on top of fund costs
questions.why: Insurance wrappers can add layers of fees on top of fund costs.

questions.q: What is a surrender charge?
options: A fee for leaving the contract early
questions.why: A fee for leaving the contract early.

questions.q: What are investment-linked life insurance funds called in Poland?
questions.why: UFK, ubezpieczeniowe fundusze kapitalowe (insurance capital funds).

questions.q: What should you compare before buying one?
options: Total fees, lock-up, whether you need the insurance
questions.why: Total fees, the lock-up period, and whether you actually need the insurance part.

questions.q: What is a limited partnership?
options: Passive investors fund a business a general partner runs
questions.why: A business where passive investors put in money and a general partner runs it; investors usually can lose only what they put in.

questions.q: What is a direct participation program?
options: A pooled investment passing a business's income to investors
questions.why: A pooled investment that passes a business's income and tax effects to investors, often in property or energy.

questions.q: Why are these called illiquid?
options: Money is locked in for years, hard to sell
questions.why: Money is often locked in for years with no easy way to sell.

questions.q: What are the main risks?
options: Business failure, high fees, low transparency, lock-ups
questions.why: Business failure, high fees, little transparency and long lock-ups.

questions.q: Who are these usually aimed at?
options: Experienced investors who can lock money away
questions.why: Experienced investors who can lock money away for years.

questions.q: How do you check the seller is licensed?
questions.why: Search the KNF register of supervised entities.

questions.q: What do you own when you buy a share?
options: A small piece of a company
questions.why: A small piece of ownership in a company.

questions.q: How can a shareholder make money?
questions.why: From the share price rising and from dividends the company pays.

questions.q: What is a dividend?
options: Part of profit paid to shareholders
questions.why: Part of a company's profit paid out to shareholders.

questions.q: Why does WIG20TR grow faster than WIG20?
questions.why: WIG20TR also counts reinvested dividends: 9,689.62 vs 4,204.70 on 19 Nov 2026.

questions.q: How far did CD Projekt shares fall from August 2020 to September 2022?
questions.why: About 83%, from 460.80 zl to 77.89 zl.

questions.q: Why is 'a company I know well' still risky?
options: Knowing it doesn't stop it falling or failing
questions.why: Knowing a company does not stop it from falling or failing.

questions.q: How far did the S&P 500 fall in 2007-2009 and in 2020?
questions.why: About -57% (Oct 2007 to Mar 2009) and about -34% (Feb to Mar 2020).

questions.q: When did the S&P 500 get back to its old high after each crash?
questions.why: March 2013 after the 2008 crash, and August 2020 after the 2020 crash.

questions.q: Markets fall 30% in a month. What do you do: sell, hold or buy more?
feedback: Selling locks in the loss. In 2008 and 2020 the S&P 500 later recovered its old high (Mar 2013, Aug 2020).
Holding is what recovered in past crashes, if you don't need the money soon.
Buying at lower prices can help long-term, but only with spare money and a long horizon.

questions.q: What tax do you pay on profit from selling shares in Poland?
questions.why: 19%, declared on PIT-38.
